title: Electronic Voting Machine
summary: An 8051 academic hardware prototype for candidate input, vote counting and LCD result display, including debouncing and winner/tie logic.
overview: The Electronic Voting Machine is an academic embedded-system prototype using an 8051 microcontroller. Push buttons accept votes for multiple candidates, and a 16×2 LCD presents counts and calculated results. Embedded C logic handles switch debouncing, vote counting and winner or tie detection. Hardware photographs and a Proteus schematic document the implementation.
approach: Interfaced multiple candidate push buttons with an 8051-family microcontroller and a 16×2 LCD.
Used software debouncing to account for the mechanical behaviour of the button inputs.
Implemented vote counting and result calculation in Embedded C, with logic to identify a winner or a tie.
Linked the circuit design to the breadboard implementation, using the LCD as the result-display interface.
outcomes: Assembled the academic voting-machine prototype shown in the hardware views.
Connected input handling, counting, winner/tie logic and LCD interfacing in one Embedded C implementation.

evidenceNotes: Do not carry over CV secure-system wording as a certification/security assurance.
No completed independent security assessment or election deployment is established.
problem: Turn multiple-candidate button inputs into counted votes and clear LCD results, including the cases where a winner or a tie must be displayed.
context: An 8051 academic embedded-system prototype, documented by a Proteus schematic and assembled breadboard photographs.
constraints: Button input handling and result logic both affect the displayed counts; switch debouncing is part of the prototype implementation.
The educational scope does not establish an independently assessed security model or certification for real elections.
lessons: A small embedded system can bring together physical input, maintained state and meaningful output.
Handling a tie explicitly makes result logic part of the design rather than an afterthought.
